title: mini-batch-sla-surface-sketch
content:
Purpose:
This is a working sketch to capture the surface area where small/continuous batch sizing interacts with concurrency allocation and p95 SLAs. The goal is a compact spreadsheet that operators can use to: (1) estimate cost delta when changing batching window or slotting, (2) understand which workloads risk p95 violation as arrival shape changes, and (3) prioritize simple runtime knobs for immediate wins.

Status and audience:
- Draft notes for runtime and capacity engineers.
- Assumes familiarity with existing slot/batch concepts.
- Not a final playbook; intended to seed a short spreadsheet + a one-pager for SREs and Solutions Eng.

High level intuition (short):
- Continuous batching reduces per-token compute by packing multiple requests into a shared forward. Benefit grows with mean request length and arrival overlap.
- Concurrency (number of slots / active requests) controls queueing: more concurrency reduces queueing delay but increases GPU occupancy inefficiency (more idle waiting on KV insert, context switches).
- p95 is sensitive to tail arrivals (microbursts) and to non-uniform request lengths. Simple averages understate tail risk.

Key modeling primitives to capture in sheet (columns to include):
- workload_id (string)
- mean_arrival_rate_rps (λ) -- requests per second per route
- arrival_cv (coeff var) -- captures burstiness; 1.0 ~ Poisson, >1 bursty
- mean_tokens_in (prompt_len)
- mean_tokens_out (gen_len)
- avg_service_time_ms (single request on empty batch) -- baseline forward pass for one request; measurable on hardware
- batch_window_ms (w) -- batching horizon used by runtime (continuous/bounded)
- effective_batch_size_mean -- expected # requests per batch (derived)
- device_slot_count (concurrency slots) -- active request slots per device
- p95_queue_delay_ms (model output)
- p95_total_latency_ms (model output = queue_delay + service_time)
- cost_per_minute_device ($) -- device cost allocation
- cost_per_1e6_tokens ($) -- derived metric for quick comparisons

Assumptions to make explicit in model:
1) Service time per request inside a batch scales sublinearly: t_batch(N) ≈ T_fixed + N * T_per_token_eff where T_fixed is kernel setup and T_per_token_eff is amortized. We use a back-of-envelope: T_fixed = 2 ms, T_per_req_overhead = 0.5 ms + 0.02 ms * gen_tokens.
2) Arrival process approximated by renewal process with given λ and CV. Use an M/G/c-ish approximation for queueing. For a compact sheet we use an Erlang-C style with CV correction: compute utilization ρ = λ * E[service_time] / c, then adjust p95 multiplier by burstiness (CV). (Notes below.)
3) Batching window w yields a geometric-ish expected batch size: E[N] ≈ λ * w * (1 + small correction for intra-window ordering). For very small w (<5ms) use measured microburst factor.
4) We target p95_total_latency <= SLA_ms (operator input). If p95 predicted > SLA, sheet flags route as 'at risk' and suggests knobs: increase device_slot_count or reduce batch_window or enable prefix caching.

Compact formulas to include in cells (text friendly):
- E_batch = clamp(round(λ * w), 1, max_batch)
- approx_service_time_per_req = T_fixed/E_batch + T_per_req_overhead + T_token * (prompt_len + gen_len)
- effective_service_time_for_queue = approx_service_time_per_req * E_batch (this is the service time of a batch job)
- util = λ * approx_service_time_per_req / slots
- p95_queue_delay ≈ M/M/c heuristic: if util < 0.7 then queue_delay ≈ (util^2)/(1-util) * S where S = approx_service_time_per_req * (1 + CV_adj). (This is rough; see below for correction.)

Burstiness correction (practical):
- We don't want heavy probability math in the sheet. Add a single tunable factor burst_mult = 1 + 0.5 * (arrival_cv - 1). For CV=1 (Poisson) burst_mult=1. For CV=2 burst_mult=1.5 which inflates queue delay prediction.
- p95_total = (p95_queue_delay * burst_mult) + approx_service_time_per_req

Example row (toy numbers):
- workload_id: search-small
- λ: 8 rps
- arrival_cv: 1.8
- prompt_len: 40 tokens
- gen_len: 60 tokens
- w: 20 ms -> E_batch ≈ 0.16 -> clamp to 1 (i.e., mostly singleton, not effective)
- slots: 8
- avg_service_time_per_req ≈ 2ms/1 + 0.5ms + 0.02ms*100 = 2 + 0.5 + 2 = 4.5ms
- util = 8 * 0.0045 / 8 = 0.0045 -> very low util -> queue negligible
- p95_total ≈ ~4.5ms -> SLA ok.

Edge case example (large gen, bursty)
- workload_id: long-doc
- λ: 1.2 rps
- arrival_cv: 2.2
- prompt_len: 20 tokens
- gen_len: 800 tokens
- w: 50ms -> E_batch ≈ 0.06 -> clamp 1 (but note if λ spikes microbursts will accumulate in a single batch window on routing)
- slots: 2
- avg_service_time_per_req ≈ 2ms + 0.5 + 0.02*820 ≈ 2 + 0.5 + 16.4 = 18.9ms
- util = 1.2 * 0.0189 / 2 ≈ 0.01134 -> still low but since gen time is high p95 dominated by service, and bursts (CV=2.2) can push queueing to multiple slots causing spike.

Why small windows sometimes hurt:
- If E_batch < 1 the batch machinery adds fixed overheads without packing benefit. Tiny windows are only useful for very high λ where E_batch > 1. For low λ, increase slots to allow concurrent singletons rather than forcing microbatching.

Simple recommendation knobs (first 3 to try):
1) Per-route batch_window_ms: start at 2/λ (ms) clipped to [5, 200]. Quick wins for mid-high λ.
2) device_slot_count: set by target util band 30% - 60% for p95 headroom. If predicted util > 60% at current slots, increase slots (adds cost).
3) burst_guard: a runtime switch that temporarily reduces batch_window_ms during detected microbursts (short-term CV spike).

Sheet UX ideas (columns + conditional coloring):
- green if p95_total < SLA*0.8, yellow if between 0.8 and 1.0, red if > SLA.
- add a small sparkline column with recent 5-minute λ to indicate upward trend.
- clickable suggested action: dropdown [increase slots | shrink window | enable burst_guard | enable prefix_cache].

Experiment plan (short):
- Select 3 routes: low-latency high λ, low λ long-gen, and bursty enterprise route. Backfill from last 7 days traces.
- Run offline spreadsheet predictions vs actual p95 observed when toggling window and slots in staging. Compare predicted p95 vs measured. Adjust T_fixed and T_per_token params per-device.
- Target: bring prediction error to <= 20% for p95 across routes.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Better queue model: can we afford an M/G/c simulation in backend to produce a single p95 per route instead of the cheap heuristic? Cost and latency of running sim per-minute needs evaluation.
- How to incorporate KV cache hits (short-circuit reduces gen time) cleanly in the spreadsheet.
- Measurement plan: collect service-time distribution per route by payload length slices.

Notes to self:
- Keep sheet small; operators prefer actionable rules over long math.
- Will pair with Maya to instrument p95 breakdown (queue vs service) in traces.
- Slack thread: #runtime-batching for quick feedback.

End.
